intro: Edinburgh is one of the few UK cities where a wet room can genuinely add value to a property rather than simply modernise it. With a housing stock dominated by Georgian townhouses, Victorian terraces, and solid stone tenement flats, homeowners across the city are increasingly turning to wet room installations as a way to bring a period property into the 21st century without compromising its character. Done well, a wet room feels like it belongs — clean lines, quality materials, and a shower space that works with the architecture rather than fighting it. Whether you're in Stockbridge, Morningside, or the New Town, the demand for skilled, experienced installation work is high, and for good reason.
localContext: Edinburgh's building stock presents specific challenges that you won't find in a city full of newer builds. Georgian townhouses and period properties typically have solid stone walls, original timber joists, and floor structures that weren't designed with wet rooms in mind. That means proper waterproofing isn't just good practice — it's essential. A tanking system needs to be specified and applied correctly to protect floors that in many cases sit above finished plasterwork or original cornicing on the ceiling below. Edinburgh also sits in a moderately hard water area, which is worth factoring in when choosing your fixtures and finishes. Hard water deposits can dull stone tiles and block shower heads more quickly, so fitting a quality inline filter or opting for materials that are easier to maintain will save you hassle further down the line. A local installer who understands Edinburgh's property types will know how to spec a job that lasts, rather than one that looks good on day one but causes problems within a few years.
serviceDetail: A wet room installation is a more involved process than a standard shower enclosure, and it's worth understanding what the work actually entails before anyone lifts a tile. The first stage is a thorough survey of the existing bathroom or space, assessing the floor structure, drainage options, and wall construction. In Edinburgh's older properties this often throws up surprises — uneven floors, lime plaster walls, or joists running in awkward directions — so this survey stage is genuinely important, not just a box-ticking exercise. Once the design is agreed, the existing bathroom is stripped back to the structure. The floor is then prepared to create a fall towards the drain — typically around 1.5–2% gradient — which may involve building up a screed or using a pre-formed wet room former depending on the floor type. Tanking comes next: a waterproof membrane is applied to all walls and the floor within the wet zone, usually extending at least 500mm beyond the shower area. This is the stage that separates a long-lasting wet room from one that causes damp problems in a year or two. After tanking is cured and checked, tiling or surface finishes are applied, followed by the fitting of the drain, shower valve, screen if required, and all sanitaryware. Finally, silicon sealing and grouting complete the waterproofed envelope. Most installations in Edinburgh properties take five to eight working days depending on complexity.
pricing: In Edinburgh, wet room installations typically run from around £6,000 at the lower end for a straightforward conversion in a newer-build property, up to £12,000 or more for a full wet room in a Georgian townhouse or period flat where structural work, specialist waterproofing, and high-end finishes are involved. The main factors affecting your quote are the size of the space, the condition of the existing floor structure, the specification of tiles and fixtures, and whether any reconfiguration of pipework or drainage is needed. Properties in the New Town, Morningside, or Bruntsfield with original features to protect around tend to sit at the higher end. Always get a detailed, itemised quote rather than a single headline figure.
whyLocal: Choosing a tradesperson who knows Edinburgh matters more for wet rooms than almost any other bathroom job. Local installers will have worked in Georgian tenements, stone-walled townhouses, and listed buildings before — they understand the quirks of the city's older properties and know what to look for before problems arise. They'll also have established relationships with local building control where notifications are required, and they'll know which suppliers carry the materials best suited to Edinburgh's building types. When something unexpected comes up mid-job — and in a period property it often does — experience with Edinburgh's housing stock is what keeps the project on track.

faqs.q: Do I need planning permission or building warrants for a wet room in Edinburgh?
faqs.a: In most cases you won't need planning permission for an internal wet room conversion. However, in Edinburgh you may need a building warrant if structural changes are involved or if the property is listed. Your installer should be able to advise you, and it's always worth checking with City of Edinburgh Council if there's any doubt before work starts.

faqs.q: Can a wet room be installed in an Edinburgh tenement flat?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's done regularly across the city. The key considerations are the floor construction — many tenement floors are timber joists — and getting the waterproofing absolutely right to protect the flat below. A specialist wet room installer with experience in Edinburgh tenements will know how to handle this properly, often using a wet room former system rather than a screed to minimise weight and depth.

faqs.q: How do I protect tiles and fittings from hard water damage in Edinburgh?
faqs.a: Edinburgh's moderately hard water can leave limescale deposits on tiles, screens, and shower heads over time. Specifying a quality inline scale filter on your shower feed helps significantly. Choosing larger format tiles with fewer grout lines also reduces the surface area where deposits build up. Your installer can advise on sealants and easy-clean coatings that make ongoing maintenance much more manageable.

faqs.q: How long does a wet room installation take in a typical Edinburgh property?
faqs.a: Most installations take between five and eight working days, though period properties in Edinburgh sometimes run longer if the survey reveals unexpected structural issues or if bespoke tiling work is involved. You'll typically be without use of that bathroom for the full duration, so it's worth planning for an alternative if it's your only facility. A good installer will give you a realistic programme before work begins.
